SCIENCE: A particle in an infinite square well of width L (0 < x < L) is prepared at t = 0 in the normalized state ψ = (φ₁ + φ₂)/√2, where φₙ(x) = √(2/L) sin(nπx/L). What is ⟨x⟩ at t = 0?

SCIENCE.source: original question written for this suite
SCIENCE.reference: standard infinite-well matrix elements (e.g. Griffiths, Introduction to Quantum Mechanics, ch. 2)
SCIENCE.derivation: ⟨x⟩ = ½(⟨x⟩₁₁ + ⟨x⟩₂₂) + Re⟨φ₁|x|φ₂⟩ = L/2 + ⟨φ₁|x|φ₂⟩, and ⟨φ₁|x|φ₂⟩ = (2/L)∫x sin(πx/L) sin(2πx/L)dx = −16L/(9π²) ≈ −0.180 L, so ⟨x⟩ = 0.320 L. Distractors: 0.500 L drops the cross term; 0.680 L flips its sign; 0.410 L halves it.

SCIENCE: A mole of non-interacting two-level systems has non-degenerate levels at energies 0 and ε. As the temperature varies, the molar heat capacity C(T) passes through a single maximum. What is that maximum value, in units of R?

SCIENCE.source: original question written for this suite
SCIENCE.reference: the Schottky anomaly (e.g. Kittel & Kroemer, Thermal Physics, ch. 3)
SCIENCE.derivation: With x = ε/kT, C/R = x² eˣ/(1 + eˣ)². Setting d/dx = 0 gives 2 = x·tanh(x/2), solved numerically x ≈ 2.399, where C/R ≈ 0.439. Distractors: 0.250 is the x² coefficient of the high-temperature expansion, and 0.500 and 0.693 (ln 2, the high-temperature entropy per system) are the usual guesses.

SCIENCE: A proton beam strikes protons at rest. What is the threshold beam kinetic energy for the reaction p + p → p + p + π⁰? Use m_p = 938.27 MeV/c² and m_π⁰ = 134.98 MeV/c².

SCIENCE.source: original question written for this suite
SCIENCE.reference: relativistic threshold kinematics (e.g. Griffiths, Introduction to Elementary Particles, ch. 3)
SCIENCE.derivation: Threshold: invariant mass √s = 2m_p + m_π. Fixed target: s = 2m_p² + 2m_pE_beam, so T = E_beam − m_p = ((2m_p + m_π)² − 4m_p²)/(2m_p) = 2m_π + m_π²/(2m_p) = 269.96 + 9.71 = 279.7 MeV. Distractors: m_π (no recoil energy), 2m_π (drops the m_π²/2m_p term), 4m_π.

SCIENCE: A woman's mother is an obligate carrier of an X-linked recessive disorder, and her father is unaffected. She has three sons, none of whom is affected. Ignoring new mutations, what is the probability that she is a carrier?

SCIENCE.source: original question written for this suite
SCIENCE.reference: Bayesian carrier-risk calculation (e.g. Young, Introduction to Risk Calculation in Genetic Counseling)
SCIENCE.derivation: Prior 1/2. P(3 unaffected sons | carrier) = (1/2)³ = 1/8; P(… | non-carrier) = 1. Posterior = (½·⅛)/(½·⅛ + ½·1) = 1/9 ≈ 11.1%. Distractors: the prior 50%, the conditional-probability term alone 12.5%, and 6.25% = (1/2)⁴.

SCIENCE: An X-ray photon of wavelength 0.0711 nm scatters from a free electron initially at rest and is detected at 90° to its original direction. What is the kinetic energy of the recoil electron? (hc = 1239.84 eV·nm; the Compton wavelength h/mₑc = 2.4263 × 10⁻³ nm.)

SCIENCE.source: original question written for this suite
SCIENCE.reference: Compton scattering (e.g. Krane, Modern Physics, ch. 3)
SCIENCE.derivation: λ′ = λ + (h/mₑc)(1 − cos 90°) = 0.0711 + 0.0024263 = 0.0735263 nm. T = hc/λ − hc/λ′ = 17437.97 − 16862.53 eV = 575.4 eV = 0.575 keV. Distractors: half and double that value, and 17.4 keV (the whole incident photon energy).

SCIENCE: A pure sample of a parent isotope with half-life 10.0 h decays to a daughter with half-life 2.00 h, and the daughter's own product is stable. Starting with no daughter nuclei, at what time is the daughter's activity largest?

SCIENCE.source: original question written for this suite
SCIENCE.reference: Bateman equations, transient equilibrium (e.g. Krane, Introductory Nuclear Physics, ch. 6)
SCIENCE.derivation: N₂(t) = λ₁N₁(0)/(λ₂ − λ₁)·(e^(−λ₁t) − e^(−λ₂t)); dN₂/dt = 0 gives t = ln(λ₂/λ₁)/(λ₂ − λ₁) with λ₁ = ln2/10, λ₂ = ln2/2: ln5/(0.2773 h⁻¹) = 5.80 h. The activity λ₂N₂ peaks at the same instant. Distractors: the mean of the half-lives (6.00 h), ln(λ₂/λ₁)/(λ₁ + λ₂) (3.87 h), ln(λ₂/λ₁)/λ₁ (23.2 h).

SCIENCE: An enzyme obeys Michaelis–Menten kinetics with Vmax = 100 μmol/min and Km = 2.0 mM. A purely competitive inhibitor is present at 10 μM (Ki = 5.0 μM) and the substrate concentration is 4.0 mM. What is the initial reaction rate?

SCIENCE.source: original question written for this suite
SCIENCE.reference: enzyme inhibition kinetics (e.g. Fersht, Structure and Mechanism in Protein Science, ch. 3)
SCIENCE.derivation: Competitive inhibition raises Km to Km(1 + [I]/Ki) = 2.0 × 3 = 6.0 mM with Vmax unchanged, so v = 100·4.0/(6.0 + 4.0) = 40.0 μmol/min. Distractors: 66.7 (uninhibited), 28.6 (uncompetitive form), 22.2 (noncompetitive form).

SCIENCE: 2,3,4-Pentanetriol (CH₃–CHOH–CHOH–CHOH–CH₃) has three carbons that bear an OH group. How many stereoisomers does it have in total, counting each enantiomer separately?

SCIENCE.source: original question written for this suite
SCIENCE.reference: stereochemistry of molecules with a pseudoasymmetric centre (e.g. Eliel & Wilen, Stereochemistry of Organic Compounds, ch. 4)
SCIENCE.derivation: Draw the chain as a Fischer projection with OH on the left (−) or right (+) at C2, C3, C4: eight labelings (a, b, c). A 180° in-plane rotation is the same molecule and maps (a, b, c) to (−c, −b, −a): no labeling is fixed (b = −b is impossible), so the eight pair up into 4 distinct molecules: two meso forms (a = c) and one enantiomeric pair. Distractors: 8 is the naive 2³, 2 and 6 the common slips.

SCIENCE: The pure rotational spectrum of ¹²C¹⁶O (atomic masses 12.000 u and 15.995 u) shows equally spaced lines separated by 3.845 cm⁻¹. Treating the molecule as a rigid rotor, what is its bond length? (h = 6.62607 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, c = 2.99792 × 10¹⁰ cm/s, 1 u = 1.66054 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.)

SCIENCE.source: original question written for this suite
SCIENCE.reference: rigid-rotor microwave spectroscopy (e.g. Atkins, Physical Chemistry, rotational spectra)
SCIENCE.derivation: Line spacing = 2B, so B = 1.9225 cm⁻¹. μ = 12.000·15.995/27.995 u = 6.8563 u. r = √(h/(8π²cμB)) = 1.131 Å. Distractors: using the spacing as B (0.80 Å), halving B (1.60 Å), and a factor-of-two slip in r (2.26 Å).

SCIENCE: How many distinct LS spectroscopic terms ²ˢ⁺¹L arise from the electron configuration d² (two equivalent electrons in one d subshell), counting each term once?

SCIENCE.source: original question written for this suite
SCIENCE.reference: term symbols of equivalent electrons under the Pauli principle (e.g. Atkins, Physical Chemistry, atomic spectra)
SCIENCE.derivation: d² has C(10,2) = 45 microstates. Tabulating (M_L, M_S) and peeling off terms leaves ³F (21), ³P (9), ¹G (9), ¹D (5), ¹S (1) = 45: five terms. The non-equivalent (d¹d¹) case would give ten (both spins for each of S, P, D, F, G). Distractors: 10 is that non-equivalent count; 8 and 9 miscount the allowed terms.

SCIENCE: A particle of mass m in an infinite square well 0 < x < L is perturbed by H′ = V₀ δ(x − L/2). What is the first-order shift in the energy of the n = 2 state?

SCIENCE.source: original question written for this suite
SCIENCE.reference: first-order non-degenerate perturbation theory (e.g. Griffiths, Introduction to Quantum Mechanics, ch. 7)
SCIENCE.derivation: E⁽¹⁾ = ⟨ψ₂|H′|ψ₂⟩ = V₀|ψ₂(L/2)|² = V₀(2/L)sin²(π) = 0, because the n = 2 state has a node at the centre. Distractors: 2V₀/L is the n = odd result, V₀/L and 4V₀/L are mis-normalizations.

SCIENCE: A van der Waals gas has critical temperature Tc = 150.0 K. What is its Boyle temperature, the temperature at which the second virial coefficient vanishes?

SCIENCE.source: original question written for this suite
SCIENCE.reference: van der Waals critical constants and virial expansion (e.g. Atkins, Physical Chemistry, real gases)
SCIENCE.derivation: B₂(T) = b − a/(RT) = 0 gives T_B = a/(Rb); the critical point is Tc = 8a/(27Rb), so T_B = (27/8)Tc = 506 K. Distractors: 44 K (8/27 inverted), 150 K (Tc itself), 1013 K (the maximum inversion temperature 2a/(Rb) = (27/4)Tc).
